extracted.intended_audience: Authors of systematic reviews of interventions (Cochrane review authors / review teams)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for specifying, grouping and synthesizing interventions, comparisons, outcomes, and eligible study designs when planning and conducting systematic reviews of interventions. Emphasises pre-specification in protocols, sensible grouping/lumping vs splitting, handling multi-component interventions, outcomes selection/prioritization, and study-design eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of intervention taxonomies/classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Interventions may be categorized using generic taxonomies (e.g. the behaviour change technique (BCT) taxonomy, behaviour change wheel) or condition/intervention-specific taxonomies (e.g. ProFaNE for falls prevention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use existing, appropriate taxonomies to describe and group interventions; examples include BCT to categorize elements like goal setting and social support, the behaviour change wheel to group by function (educate, persuade, enable), and ProFaNE to specify broad groups and subgroups (exercise: gait, balance, flexibility). Some Cochrane Groups recommend specific taxonomies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide between 'lumping' and 'splitting' interventions for synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to pool all interventions in a single meta-analysis ('lumping') with exploration of effect modifiers, or to synthesise specific interventions separately ('splitting').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the analytic approach that answers the review question and is interpretable. 'Lumping' can address broad questions but may mask heterogeneity; 'splitting' answers narrower questions but may leave too few studies for synthesis. Examples: combined exercise categories for knee osteoarthritis with subgroup analyses; see Chapter 2, Section 2.3.2 for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to multi-component or co-interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify how interventions that include multiple components (complex interventions) or co-interventions will be treated: components might be eligible alone, only when combined, or treated as multi-component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include: (1) identifying components for meta-regression or components-based network meta-analysis; (2) grouping based on the 'main' component; (3) specifying a separate 'multi-component interventions' group; (4) reporting results study-by-study; or (5) excluding multi-component interventions if the effect of interest can't be discerned. Discuss pros/cons: lumping multi-component interventions can show general effects but may cause heterogeneity and inability to isolate effective components. Examples provided (psychological therapies, smoking cessation reviews). See Chapter 11 and cited methodological papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group interventions by main component when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When one component predominates or is the intervention of primary interest, categorize multi-component interventions by that main component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: psychoeducation + CBT categorized as CBT when CBT is the main eligible therapy. This simplifies grouping but should be justified and prespecified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify a separate group for multi-component interventions (if used)
rubrics_metrics.description: Option to treat multi-component interventions as their own category to capture their combined effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be used alongside lumped analyses and separate meta-analyses for single components. Categorization of multi-component interventions may still be based on the main component for separate analyses. Example: psychosocial interventions for smoking cessation used both combined meta-analysis and separate meta-analyses with main-component categorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build contingencies by specifying intervention groupings at multiple levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan grouping of interventions at more than one level (specific and broader groups) to retain flexibility for synthesis if few studies are identified for narrowly defined groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predefining both narrow and broader groupings allows synthesis even when data are sparse. Example: group any psychosocial intervention as a single comparison but also present separate meta-analyses for specific types when data permit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define planned comparisons between intervention groups
rubrics_metrics.description: For each synthesis, explicitly define which intervention groups will be compared (e.g. intervention vs placebo, intervention vs control, intervention A vs intervention B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard meta-analysis typically compares two groups at a time. Choose a subset of possible comparisons that address the most important clinical and research questions; compare novel interventions against established practice where relevant. Examples and types of comparisons (placebo/sham, control/usual care, A vs B including dose/timing differences) are given. Placebo vs control distinction may be arbitrary and groups may be combined when similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for co-interventions (supplementary interventions present in both arms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate cases where the same supplementary intervention is delivered alongside the intervention of interest in both arms (e.g. aromatherapy + massage vs massage alone) and plan how to handle this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If supplementary intervention is unimportant it can be ignored; otherwise plan for possible interaction (synergy or antagonism) that may increase heterogeneity. Statistical approaches include using random-effects meta-analysis to encompass heterogeneity or subgroup analyses to assess effect modification by the supplementary intervention. See Chapter 10 sections referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting review outcomes (do not usually use outcomes to determine eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad outcome domains are decided at PICO stage; reporting of outcomes should rarely determine study eligibility because excluding studies for unreported outcomes risks selective reporting bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies should not be excluded because they do not report a particular outcome; exceptions exist when the review specifically addresses prevention of a particular outcome or an intervention purpose tied to an outcome (e.g. adverse effects). See MECIR Box 3.2.d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify role of outcomes (MECIR C8: Clarifying role of outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify in advance whether outcomes listed under 'Criteria for considering studies' are used as inclusion criteria or merely as outcomes of interest among included studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcome measures should not always form part of inclusion criteria, but if they do, ensure outcomes are truly absent rather than unreported. This is a mandatory expectation for intervention reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predefine outcome domains (MECIR C14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define in advance outcomes that are critical to the review and any additional important outcomes, specifying domains and measures in full to reduce selective outcome reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical outcomes should be few (normally reflect at least one benefit and one harm) and the review conclusions should be based largely on effects on these outcomes. Up to seven critical and important outcomes will form the basis of GRADE assessment and be summarized in abstract and summaries, although the review may measure more. This is mandatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose outcomes important to users (MECIR C15)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select only outcomes that are critical or important to users of the review (healthcare consumers, professionals, policy makers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established core outcome sets where available; include patient-reported outcomes where possible; consider resource use and costs. Avoid large numbers of trivial outcomes that make reviews unfocused and prone to selective reporting bias. This is mandatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predefine acceptable outcome measures (MECIR C16)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, define in advance what will constitute acceptable outcome measures (diagnostic criteria, scales, composite outcomes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predefining measures reduces selective reporting bias. It may be difficult to predefine adverse effects. This is highly desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predefine how to choose among multiple outcome measures (MECIR C17)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify in advance how outcome measures will be selected when multiple possible measures exist (different definitions, assessors, scales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pre-specified hierarchy guards against selective reporting. Provide rationale for choice. Predefining choices is highly desirable; selection procedures should be independent of study results and documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predefine outcome time points of interest (MECIR C18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define in advance timing of outcome measurement (e.g. short-term, medium-term, long-term) and consider grouping time points into intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prespecification guards against selective outcome reporting. Choose clinically meaningful time frames and consider width (narrow may lead to few studies; broad may cause multiplicity). This is highly desirable. Examples given for short-term (≤6 months) and long-term (>6 months) outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure outcomes are meaningful to decision makers
rubrics_metrics.description: Include outcomes likely to be meaningful to clinicians, patients, the public, administrators and policy makers (e.g. survival, clinical events, patient-reported outcomes, adverse events, burdens, economic outcomes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude trivial or meaningless outcomes. Be cautious with surrogate/interim outcomes: they can mislead as they may not predict clinically important outcomes. Use various sources (consumers, advisory groups, literature, core outcome sets) to develop outcome lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize outcomes for summaries and GRADE assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: After compiling relevant outcomes, prioritize them into 'critical', 'important' and 'not important' for decision making; critical outcomes form the basis of 'Summary of findings' and GRADE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify outcomes at protocol stage; include no more than seven outcomes in 'Summary of findings' tables; do not choose outcomes based on anticipated or observed effect sizes or ease of availability in primary studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fully specify outcome domains for categorization (Table 3.2.c Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each outcome domain, provide a short label and describe the domain sufficiently to enable categorizing eligible outcomes from included studies, basing definitions on the construct measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define domains hierarchically (broad groups → domains → narrower domains → specific measures). Consider existing terminology, list examples for inconsistently labelled outcomes, and consider implications of grouping level for heterogeneity vs feasibility of synthesis. Use causal models/logic models where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine and use existing systems/core outcome sets (Table 3.2.c Step 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether an existing system for outcome identification/grouping exists (COMET, ICHOM, Cochrane group outcome sets, taxonomies) and use these when available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use core outcome sets to standardize labels and facilitate grouping and comparison across studies and reviews. Examples: COMET database, Cochrane Pregnancy & Childbirth core set, IPDAS criteria for decision aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define outcome timing (Table 3.2.c Step 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify the timing of measurement for each outcome domain, often using time frames rather than exact points (e.g. 'short-term', 'medium-term', 'long-term').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on clinically meaningful times; consider accepted standards in the area; decide on width of time frames; provide rationale and examples (e.g. antidepressant treatment duration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify measurement tools/methods and minimum measurement quality (Table 3.2.c Step 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each outcome domain, specify acceptable measurement methods/tools and consider whether different methods are comparable for synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimum inclusion criteria may include evidence of reliability and validity; for self-reported measures, ensure items cover the domain and have theoretical/empirical basis and consumer involvement. Identify measures from core outcome sets or systematic reviews of instruments (e.g. COSMIN). Examples include distinguishing biochemically validated vs self-report smoking cessation measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-specify how to handle multiplicity of outcomes within studies (Table 3.2.c Step 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate multiple outcomes/measures/time points per study and prespecify a method to select or account for these to avoid dependent effect estimates and selective choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options: select one outcome per study (using a pre-specified, result-independent hierarchy) or use meta-analysis methods that account for dependency (multivariate meta-analysis, multilevel models, robust variance estimation). Document all eligible measures in 'Characteristics of included studies' and state which was selected and why. Provide example hierarchies and selection procedures (blinded selection, sample-size/primary-outcome/median-effect rules). Note multiplicity from multiple analyses or multiple reports and plan for these.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan synthesis method for outcome domains (Table 3.2.c Step 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how to synthesize when different measurement methods/tools have been used across studies: synthesize together, separately, or include all using methods that model dependency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options and trade-offs: (a) combine measures of same domain to maximize synthesis potential, using subgroup/sensitivity analyses to check robustness (may increase heterogeneity; consider random-effects models); (b) conduct separate meta-analyses for each instrument (may create interpretation problems and inflate type I error); (c) include all effect estimates using multivariate/multilevel/robust variance estimation methods to account for dependency. Examples: sensitivity analyses excluding self-report vs biochemical outcomes; multilevel modelling for many effects per study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build contingencies by specifying both specific and broader outcome domains (Table 3.2.c Step 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify outcome groupings at different levels so that broader domains can be used for synthesis if narrow domains lack sufficient data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flexibility prevents inability to synthesize when few studies report specific measures. Example: specify BMI as specific outcome and 'indicator of body mass' as broader domain (weight, waist circumference) to facilitate synthesis when BMI data are sparse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predefine eligible study designs (MECIR C9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define in advance eligibility criteria for study designs in a clear and unambiguous way, focusing on study features rather than ambiguous design labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predefining study designs is mandatory. Consider which designs provide reliable data for the review objectives, especially when including non-randomized studies. Clarify features that determine eligibility (e.g. randomization, control groups, follow-up) rather than using labels alone.
